title: India Needs Faster Growth and Stronger Rupee to Hit $20 Trillion by 2036: Report
excerpt: Brokerage Equirus lays out a 20-step reform agenda spanning GST, GCCs, and capital markets to bridge the gap between India's $3.7 trillion economy and the $20 trillion target.
body:
• Brokerage Equirus says India could reach $20 trillion GDP by 2036, requiring underlying rupee growth of 14.2% and annual currency appreciation of 3-3.6%
  • India's $3.7 trillion economy would need to expand roughly 5.5 times, sustaining nominal dollar growth of about 18% annually — well above the 10-11% historical trend
  • A 20-step reform agenda targeting GST, capital markets, GCCs, and human capital could generate Rs 4.5 trillion in net annual economic gains

India could become a $20 trillion economy by 2036, but getting there will require a sustained growth rate far above historical trends and a significantly stronger rupee, according to a research report by domestic brokerage Equirus.

Currently estimated at around $3.7 trillion, India's economy would need to expand roughly 5.5 times in a decade. That means sustaining nominal dollar growth of about 18% a year, compared with the 10-11% rate the country has averaged historically, the brokerage said.

Services Must Lead the Way

The report argues that the composition of India's growth will matter as much as its pace. Services, which currently account for about 54% of GDP, would need to contribute more than 65% as India approaches the $20 trillion milestone. The sector's economic output would have to rise from roughly $2 trillion to more than $11 trillion.

Manufacturing could face headwinds from an increasingly protectionist global trade environment, while agriculture's share of GDP is expected to decline as urbanization accelerates.

India has already demonstrated the capacity for rapid acceleration. It took 67 years after independence to build its first $2 trillion economy, but the economy nearly doubled during the decade following 2014.

A 20-Step Reform Blueprint

Equirus has proposed a sweeping reform package spanning the real economy, capital markets, human capital, services, and urban governance. Key measures include bringing fuel under the GST regime, setting minimum capital-expenditure floors for states, listing the Railways, creating an Indian sovereign fund, expanding private education capacity, and reviving private-sector R&D.

On the financial side, the report calls for deeper corporate bond markets and reforms to reduce tax-related working-capital pressures. Equirus estimates that abolishing advance tax could release around Rs 10 trillion in working capital, while moving to a flat 5% TDS could unlock another Rs 13.4 trillion.

GCCs and Tourism as Growth Engines

The report puts particular emphasis on global capability centers (GCCs). A proposed National GCC policy could increase the number of GCCs in India from more than 1,800 to 5,000, potentially generating an economic impact of $470-600 billion and creating 20-25 million jobs, Equirus estimated.

"Tourism is another area identified as having significant potential, with greater promotion potentially adding around $21 billion a year in foreign exchange receipts."

— Equirus Research Report

Overall, Equirus estimates its reform package could generate about Rs 7.9 trillion in annual direct gains against costs of roughly Rs 3.4 trillion, yielding a net annual benefit of Rs 4.5 trillion.

Execution Is Everything

The report cautions that reaching $20 trillion will depend on execution across multiple fronts simultaneously rather than any single policy lever. Sustaining rapid growth while improving the rupee's external value and expanding high-productivity services will be central to India's ability to meet the 2036 target.

For global investors, the trajectory matters as much as the destination. At $20 trillion, India would rank among the world's three largest economies — a shift that would reshape global capital flows, trade patterns, and the competitive landscape for multinational corporations operating in the region.
